narration: Picture the open ocean, roughly ten million years ago. A baleen whale about the length of a school bus is cruising near the surface. It has little reason to fear the sharks around it. But something is rising from the dark water below. Something with teeth longer than your forearm.

This is Livyatan, a giant relative of the modern sperm whale, and one of the most powerful predators ever to hunt with teeth. In the next few minutes we will look at how it was found, how it was built, what it ate, and why it disappeared.

Our story starts not in the sea, but in a desert. The Pisco Formation on the southern coast of Peru is one of the richest marine fossil sites on Earth. This dry, wind-scoured land was once seafloor, and today it gives up the bones of whales, seals, sharks, and even sloths that swam in the sea.

In 2008, a team working at a site called Cerro Colorado uncovered a skull. Not a small one. It measured about three metres (ten feet) from end to end, and both its upper and lower jaws still held massive teeth.

The team, led by palaeontologist Olivier Lambert, described the animal in 2010. They first named it Leviathan, after the sea monster of legend. But that name had already been given to another animal, an extinct relative of elephants, so the genus became Livyatan, the Hebrew form of the word. The species name, melvillei, honours Herman Melville, the author of Moby-Dick. A fitting tribute for a whale that may have hunted other whales.

So how big was it? Only the skull and teeth are known, so the body has to be estimated by comparison with living sperm whales. Most estimates fall between 13.5 and 17.5 metres, or roughly 44 to 57 feet. That is in the same league as a large male sperm whale today.

The resemblance ends at the mouth. A modern sperm whale has a long, narrow lower jaw and feeds mainly by suction, swallowing squid in the deep. Its upper jaw has few working teeth. Livyatan was different. It carried big, interlocking teeth in both jaws, set in a short, wide snout built for gripping and tearing.
And those teeth were enormous. The largest were more than 36 centimetres, or about 14 inches, long. Leaving tusks aside, they are among the largest biting teeth of any animal ever discovered.

On top of the skull sits a deep hollow called the supracranial basin. In living sperm whales, a similar basin holds the spermaceti organ, so Livyatan probably had one too. What that organ did is still debated. It may have focused sound for echolocation, helping the whale find prey in murky water. Some researchers have even suggested it worked as a cushion for ramming, although that idea is controversial.

With jaws like these, Livyatan was almost certainly not slurping up squid. Its most likely prey were baleen whales, which were common in these seas. Many were medium-sized, perhaps seven to ten metres, or 23 to 33 feet, long.

The teeth themselves offer clues. Many are heavily worn where upper and lower teeth ground past each other, the mark of an animal that bit hard and often. A large hollow on the side of the skull anchored the jaw-closing muscles, hinting at a very powerful bite.

A likely strategy was to approach from below or behind, seize the prey with a short, crushing bite, and hold on until it weakened. Nobody has watched Livyatan hunt, so this is a reconstruction, but it fits the anatomy. In a way, it played a role similar to killer whales today, only on a far larger scale.

Livyatan was not the only giant in those waters. The same rocks in Peru also contain teeth of megalodon, the enormous prehistoric shark. The two predators probably overlapped in time and place, and both seem to have targeted mid-sized whales.

Did they fight? There is no direct evidence of that. It is more likely that they competed for the same food. It is tempting to imagine an epic battle between them, but the fossils only tell us that they were neighbours, not who would have won.
So why did Livyatan vanish? We do not have a clear answer. Its fossil record is thin, and the best-dated remains come from a narrow slice of time around nine to ten million years ago.

One idea is that its menu changed. As the climate cooled towards the end of the Miocene, ocean ecosystems were reshaped. Many of the mid-sized baleen whales it relied on declined, while others grew larger. A specialist predator can struggle when its prey changes. Isolated teeth from places such as Chile, South Africa and Australia suggest giant raptorial sperm whales were once widespread, but in the end this lineage of whale hunters faded away.

Today, the sperm whale is the last giant of its family, a deep-diving squid hunter rather than a killer of whales. But long ago, its cousin Livyatan cruised the coast of South America as one of the most formidable predators the oceans have ever seen.
